rows.source: UKHSA listeriosis prevention and clinical management
rows.verified: Listeria monocytogenes is a foodborne pathogen associated particularly with contaminated chilled and ready-to-eat foods.

rows.source: UKHSA listeriosis prevention and clinical management
rows.verified: The incubation period can range from about 24 hours to 70 days, so delayed presentation is possible.

rows.source: UKHSA listeriosis prevention and clinical management
rows.verified: Pregnant people, newborns, older people and people with weakened immune systems are at increased risk of invasive listeriosis.

rows.source: UKHSA listeriosis prevention and clinical management
rows.verified: Healthcare and care facilities serving food are food-business operators and must provide safe food to patients and residents.

rows.source: UKHSA listeriosis prevention and clinical management
rows.verified: Suspected or confirmed invasive listeriosis requires clinical liaison with microbiology and treatment according to local antimicrobial protocols.

rows.source: UKHSA listeriosis prevention and clinical management
rows.verified: UKHSA enhanced surveillance follows cases to identify outbreak sources and limit further disease.

rows.source: UKHSA listeriosis prevention and clinical management
rows.verified: Listeria can grow at refrigeration temperatures but is killed by thorough cooking and pasteurisation.

rows.source: UKHSA listeriosis prevention and clinical management
rows.verified: UKHSA reported 179 listeriosis cases in England and Wales in 2024 and investigated multiple food-linked outbreaks.

rows.source: UKHSA listeriosis prevention and clinical management
rows.verified: Listeriosis risk depends on food type, contamination level, storage temperature and duration, preparation, host age, pregnancy, immunity and exposure timing.

rows.source: UKHSA listeriosis prevention and clinical management
rows.verified: UKHSA listeria evidence is food-, facility-, outbreak-, patient-, surveillance- and time-specific and is not an exact parcel-level illness probability.

rows.source: UKHSA tetanus prevention and wound management
rows.verified: Tetanus is environmentally acquired and is not transmitted from person to person.

rows.source: UKHSA tetanus prevention and wound management
rows.verified: Immunisation provides personal protection, and recovery from tetanus does not reliably produce immunity.

rows.source: UKHSA tetanus prevention and wound management
rows.verified: A complete UK tetanus vaccination course consists of 5 appropriately spaced doses.

rows.source: UKHSA tetanus prevention and wound management
rows.verified: Assessment of tetanus-prone wounds should use reliable vaccination records wherever possible.

rows.source: UKHSA tetanus prevention and wound management
rows.verified: Immediate vaccine reinforcement is recommended for some tetanus-prone wounds when the last dose was more than 10 years ago.

rows.source: UKHSA tetanus prevention and wound management
rows.verified: High-risk tetanus-prone wounds may require both a vaccine dose and human tetanus immunoglobulin at separate sites.

rows.source: UKHSA tetanus prevention and wound management
rows.verified: Point-of-care tetanus antibody testing is not recommended for routine wound assessment because evidence on clinical benefit and performance is limited.

rows.source: UKHSA tetanus prevention and wound management
rows.verified: Older under-immunised adults have represented an important risk group among reported UK tetanus cases.

rows.source: UKHSA tetanus prevention and wound management
rows.verified: Tetanus risk depends on wound type and contamination, tissue damage, foreign material, vaccination history, age, immune response and treatment timing.

rows.source: UKHSA tetanus prevention and wound management
rows.verified: UKHSA tetanus evidence is wound-, patient-, vaccine-, treatment-, clinical- and time-specific and is not an exact parcel-level disease probability.
